content: Chelating agents, despite being included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, are not widely available in many lowand middle-income countries. The WHO plans to use its guidance to advocate for improved access to these agents as part of universal health coverage and to enhance the procurement of essential medicines through inter-country collaboration. In the area of nutritional interventions, the WHO is developing guidelines for single and multi-nutrient supplementation to improve the health of children and pregnant women. Additionally, the WHO is collaborating with the FAO to update guidance on nutrient requirements for children. The WHO is also focusing on strengthening and establishing poison centers, which will play a key role in implementing the guidelines, as these centers are among the primary users of the recommendations. Training workshops for healthcare providers will be organized in selected countries, resources permitting, to address the identification of risk factors, diagnosis, and management of lead exposure. These workshops will be supplemented by online courses. Lead is a widely used but highly toxic metal that can cause life-threatening poisoning and long-term adverse health effects. Exposure can occur through ingestion of lead-containing substances, inhalation of fumes during occupational exposure, or contact with environmental contaminants. Individual cases of lead poisoning persist due to various sources, and mass lead-poisoning events have occurred globally, often linked to environmental or food contamination. For example, in northwest Nigeria in 2010, approximately 400 children died from environmental lead poisoning, and over 1,000 children under five years of age were treated with chelation therapy during a humanitarian response. Lead exposure remains a significant public health concern, contributing to 7 million disability-adjusted life years in 2019. Children are particularly vulnerable, with WHO estimating that lead exposure accounts for 30% of the global burden of idiopathic developmental intellectual disability. The most critical aspect of managing lead exposure is identifying and removing the source of exposure. Depending on the circumstances and severity, other management measures include gastrointestinal decontamination, nutritional supplementation, and chelation therapy to facilitate lead elimination from the body. In many countries, managing lead exposure is challenging due to limited access to laboratory services for diagnosis, chelating agents for treatment, and environmental services for source identification and remediation. Four chelating agents commonly used for lead poisoning are dimercaprol, penicillamine, sodium calcium edetate, and succimer, but these are not universally available. The purpose of the WHO guideline is to assist physicians in diagnosing and treating lead exposure in individual patients. The recommendations can also be adapted for mass poisoning incidents and used to inform national programs for diagnosing and managing lead poisoning. Other groups may use the guideline to develop their own treatment protocols. The guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations on interpreting blood lead concentrations, using gastrointestinal decontamination, employing nutritional supplementation, and administering chelating agents. However, it does not address methods for preventing lead exposure, such as environmental remediation, which will be covered in a separate guideline. The guideline was developed following the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. This process involved identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updates. The guideline was created with input from a steering group, a guideline development group, an external review group, a systematic review team, and methodologists. The guideline development group consisted of 15 external experts from six WHO regions, specializing in clinical toxicology, children’s environmental health, lead poisoning prevention and management, and public health. They reviewed the scope of the guidelines, identified and ranked outcomes, and developed systematic evidence review protocols. The systematic review team conducted evidence reviews for each intervention, collaborating with WHO technical officers and the guideline development group. Evidence profiles were constructed for each outcome, assessing the quality of evidence using the GRADE approach. The guideline also addressed conflicts of interest among contributors. All experts were required to declare relevant interests before participating in the guideline development process. Any potential conflicts were reviewed and managed according to WHO policies to ensure objectivity. The guideline development group members were selected for their expertise in lead toxicity and/or experience in managing lead exposure.
